{"id": "39:23/q18", "question": "What are the linked traditional Quranic divisions called mathānī?", "turns_on": "Different units and starting points are reported for the traditional sura divisions.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q18/p1", "position": "They are a sura group after the seven long suras and miʾūn, before the mufassal.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Ṭabarī and Burhān define miʾūn as near one hundred verses and mathānī as succeeding them. A poem lists ṭawāsīn, ḥawāmīm and mufassal; basmala divisions explain mufassal. Wāthila's report compares the four groups with Torah, Gospel, Psalms and a special gift; Burhān calls it gharīb with weak Saʿīd b. Bashīr."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p2", "position": "The seven long suras end at Yūnus.", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās list Baqara through Aʿrāf then Yūnus; Māwardī calls it correct; Ṭabarī says ʿUthmān's Anfāl/Barāʾa report does not establish those two in the seven."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p3", "position": "The seven long suras treat al-Anfāl and Barāʾa as one ending unit.", "reasons": "A poem and Burhān give this count; ʿUthmān said similar stories and absence of clarification led him to pair them without basmala. Al-Ālūsī discusses whether this reflects independent judgment or a prescribed order."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p4", "position": "The mufassal begins at Sūrat Muḥammad.", "reasons": "Māwardī attributes it to most scholars; Burhān lists it among twelve reported starting points."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p5", "position": "The mufassal begins at Qāf.", "reasons": "ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar reports this from many Companions; a report from the Thaqīf delegation says a Companion hizb began there; Burhān also lists it."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p6", "position": "The mufassal begins at al-Ḍuḥā.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās connects this beginning with Meccan takbīr between suras."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p7", "position": "Other reported mufassal starts include al-Jāthiya and al-Ḥujurāt.", "reasons": "Burhān counts twelve views and lists these alongside Muḥammad and Qāf."}, {"id": "39:23/q18/p8", "position": "Al-Fātiḥa bears the name seven mathānī.", "reasons": "Poetic evidence and its repeated prayer recitation support this title; Burhān lists it among more than twenty names."}]}

{"id": "39:23/q21", "question": "How is the clause 'their skins shiver' attached syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the listeners' response remains a modifier of the Book or begins a new statement.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q21/p1", "position": "It qualifies the Book as an adjectival clause.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and al-Samīn permit this; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no pause at mathānī on this parse."}, {"id": "39:23/q21/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause for the Book.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Ālūsī report this analysis."}, {"id": "39:23/q21/p3", "position": "It begins an independent sentence about the Book's effects.", "reasons": "Ālūsī prefers the transition after the Book's attributes; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says one may pause at mathānī on this parse."}]}
{"id": "39:23/q22", "question": "Is skin shivering literal or a figure for fear?", "turns_on": "Whether the bodily sign is an observed reaction or figurative depiction; several sources allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q22/p1", "position": "It is an actual bodily response to revelation and warning.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī and Ālūsī prefer a palpable effect; Ṭabarī and others describe skin reacting to heard recitation. {"id": "39:23/q23", "question": "What brings the first shiver and subsequent softening?", "turns_on": "The sources vary between a warning/mercy sequence and deeper stages of contemplation.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q23/p1", "position": "Warnings and punishment cause fear; mercy, promise and reward bring hope and softness.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, Ṭabarī and most commentators make this temporal contrast. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes awe may attract believers but burden deniers; Burhān reconciles trembling with 13:28 and 8:2 as fear of deviation within settled conviction. Ibn Jurayj explicitly pairs warning with Paradise and hoped-for mercy. Biqāʿī notes bodily outer surfaces, intense reverent fear, and remembrance of divine majesty. Qurṭubī compares the response with the mountain's splitting and humility at 59:21. Ibn ʿĀshūr says warnings move believers to avoid prohibitions, while promises make them rejoice, recognize promised good in their deeds, and expect it hopefully; the paired feelings fit their conduct to God's majesty, forbearance, and mercy."}, {"id": "39:23/q23/p2", "position": "Awe arises from contemplating divine majesty, then serenity from beauty and oneness.", "reasons": "Rāzī says initial reward-and-punishment response is only the first level: divine transcendence beyond place and pre-eternity make the mind shiver, while reasoning about unity and necessary existence brings calm; Qushayrī and Bursevī allow fear/hope, contraction/expansion, disclosure/concealment; al-Nahrjurī contrasts beginners and advanced knowers. Māwardī also describes awe followed by softness on recitation. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Fakhr quoting perfected seekers: divine majesty stuns them, then a trace of beauty revives them."}]}
{"id": "39:23/q24", "question": "Whose skins shiver in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase describes all God-fearing hearers, the Companions as exemplars, or a spiritual rank.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q24/p1", "position": "God-fearing believers, God's friends, and receptive hearers.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Qatāda and Ibn Kathīr describe friends who weep, shiver and settle. {"id": "39:23/q25", "question": "How should hearers behave when moved by recitation?", "turns_on": "Whether shivering and composure are the normative limits of sincere response, or swooning can be involuntary.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q25/p1", "position": "Weep, shiver, become calm, listen attentively and act; avoid contrived loss of control.", "reasons": "Qatāda says God's allies do not lose reason; Asma and Ibn ʿUmar contrast the Companions with collapsing hearers and blame Satan. Ibn Sīrīn proposes the rooftop or wall test; an anecdote of Moses rejects torn clothes without an opened heart. Ibn Kathīr values stillness and deliberate prostration; al-Zubayr's family and Ibrahim likewise challenge fainting and visionary claims. Rāzī reports Ghazālī's question why some swoon at love poems more than Quran; Rāzī contrasts Quranic majesty with poems of creaturely union and separation."}, {"id": "39:23/q25/p2", "position": "Involuntary swooning may reflect weak capacity, and the verse need not exclude other states.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports Sufi shaykhs' defense: weak hearts cannot bear influx, and the relative clause may concern firm saints rather than all believers. He calls swooning a deficiency in contrast to completed wayfarers, yet says involuntary reactions are not blameworthy."}]}
{"id": "39:23/q26", "question": "What benefit is reported for a shiver or tenderness from fear of God?", "turns_on": "The reports promise remission, protection from Fire, or a propitious time for supplication.", "positions": [{"id": "39:23/q26/p1", "position": "Fear-induced shivering sheds sins like leaves from a dry tree.", "reasons": "Reports through al-ʿAbbās and others repeat the image; Ibn al-Jawzī, Biqāʿī and Māwardī state no grading here."}, {"id": "39:23/q26/p2", "position": "God forbids the Fire to one whose skin shivers in fear.", "reasons": "A second report from al-ʿAbbās or Ibn ʿAbbās gives protection from Fire; Ubayy links tears from fear with that protection."}, {"id": "39:23/q26/p3", "position": "Tenderness or gooseflesh is an occasion to pray and expect a response.", "reasons": "The report of Ubayy's recitation before the Prophet says to seize tenderness for prayer; Umm a

{"id": "39:24/q01", "question": "What does يَتَّقِى mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb emphasizes protective action or meeting what comes.", "positions": [{"id": "39:24/q01/p1", "position": "To shield or protect oneself against harm, using the face as the means here.", "reasons": "ʿAntara's battle line illustrates shielding from spears (Tabrisi); Bursevi glosses اتقى بكذا as taking something for a shield; Ibn ʿAshur distinguishes waqā, with two objects and bi for the instrument, from iftiʿāl with one object, and cites al-Nābigha's hand as instrument."}, {"id": "39:24/q01/p2", "position": "To receive or meet something.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan cites a poem in which a woman raises her hand to shield herself from sight, showing this usage."}]}

{"id": "39:24/q20", "question": "What further sound changes does Sibawayh use to illustrate easing near the form يَتَّقِى?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:24/q20/p1", "position": "Frequent or difficult consonant sequences undergo substitution, assimilation, or deletion in several Arabic forms.", "reasons": "Sibawayh derives ست from سدس by substitution and assimilation, rejects ṣād there; ييجل/أدل ease wāw beside yāʾ; Tamim ود assimilates وتد but risks ambiguity, and عتدان/عدان avoid tāʾ-dāl. أحست/مست/ظلت lose a doubled consonant. يسطيع either deletes t from يستطيع or adds sīn to أطاع; يستيع either deletes ṭāʾ or replaces it with t. استخذ either substitutes sīn for t or deletes t from استتخذ. Some say الطجع for اضطجع. Frequent tribal names delete n before article l, and علماء بنو فلان loses l of على الماء."}]}

{"id": "39:24/q22", "question": "What general claims about metaphor and eloquence occur with the verse material?", "turns_on": "Which conventional likeness or semantic gain makes expression effective.", "positions": [{"id": "39:24/q22/p1", "position": "A successful metaphor or simile conveys a recognizable likeness rather than literal identity or falsehood.", "reasons": "Jurjani says a raincloud identity for 2:19 cannot recover the intended comparison, while ṣayyib may convey generosity elsewhere. Conventional traits make sun, lion and sea metaphors work; roundness is not conventionally the sun's trait, though sphere conveys it. Hyperbolic identification can call people stars or lions. He praises Abu Firas's rational arrow simile, treats 19:4 as gray spreading like fire, reports the Prophet's mirror comparison of a believer as revealing qualities, and explains green growth on dung as beauty with corrupt origin."}, {"id": "39:24/q22/p2", "position": "Truthful and meaningful verbal invention can be eloquent, whereas bare sound repetition cannot explain Quranic inimitability.", "reasons": "Jurjani rejects a demand for factual contradiction. Al-Mutanabbi's invented motive for killing enemies is to feed expectant wolves, portraying generosity; Jurjani adds that decisive victory spares future bloodshed and contrasts rage-driven killing. Abu Talib al-Maʾmuni's minister dreams of aiding a late visitor, but overexplanation weakens praise. In Dalail, a modern poet's repeated word adds meaning where Abu Tammam's repeated madhhab does not; paronomasia like najā/najā may adorn meaning, yet phonetic ease alone cannot ground Quranic inimitability."}]}
